explicitUncertainty.text:
In the **Smith–Suchanek–Williams** experiments, a small group of traders (university students, often about a dozen) trade a single asset in a computerised double auction over a fixed number of periods (15 in the standard design). At the end of each period every share pays a dividend drawn from a known distribution (in the standard design, $0, 8, 28$ or $60$ cents with equal probability, expected dividend 24 cents), and the share is worthless after the last period. So the **fundamental value** is known and **declines in a staircase**: with $n$ periods left it is $n\times$ (expected dividend), i.e. 3.60 dollars at the start and 0.24 at the last period. Instead of following that staircase, prices typically start below it, rise above it, form a **bubble** of many times the fundamental value and **crash** near the end. With **experienced** subjects (who have taken part in earlier sessions with the same market) the bubbles shrink or disappear.

Scope: the distinctive outcome of the original experiments (14 of 22 sessions with bubbles and crashes); results depend on design details (cash endowments, dividend structure, trading rules), and later studies find that bubbles are reduced by common knowledge of rationality and by experience. The dividend distribution above is from memory of the standard design and is flagged for checking.

queue.name: The heavy plough and the horse collar

explicitUncertainty.text:
The **heavy plough** has a vertical **coulter** to cut the sod, a **share** to cut it from below and a **mouldboard** to turn it over, so it opens a deep furrow in wet, heavy soils where the older scratch plough (the ard) only scored the surface. It needs a strong team. The **horse collar** is a padded, stiff ring resting on a horse's shoulders, so that the horse pulls with its chest and shoulders and not against its windpipe.

The historical claim associated with Lynn White Jr. (*Medieval Technology and Social Change*, 1962) is that these inventions, together with the horseshoe, let medieval Europe plough the heavy northern soils and raised agricultural output, and that the collar multiplied a horse's useful pull. How much of this survives is disputed. The idea that the older throat-and-girth harness choked the horse goes back to Lefebvre des Noëttes (1931), and a test attributed to him is quoted as limiting two horses to about 1100 lb against about 1½ tons for one horse in a collar (as cited by Needham). Reconstructions by Spruytte (published 1977 and 1983), working with M. Littauer, found that ancient harnesses, correctly fitted, let a horse pull nearly as much; on that view the collar's real gain was a lower point of attachment, which suited ploughing. The modest effect of the collar is also argued by Weller. I could not check the original measurements, so the two views below are presented as claims, not data.

What the picture does compute is statics. The trace from the harness to the plough's clevis is a straight line; the pull along it has a horizontal part that the soil resists and a vertical part that depends on how high the horse's attachment is above the clevis. The numbers for soil resistance and the pull of an animal are illustrative round figures.

refs: White, Medieval Technology and Social Change (Oxford: Clarendon, 1962)
Weller, Roman Traction Systems (online), and Needham (1986) as cited by Wikipedia “Horse collar”

queue.name: The canal pound lock

explicitUncertainty.text:
A **pound lock** lets a boat change level on a canal. It is a chamber with a gate at each end: the boat enters at one level, the gates are closed, water is let in or out of the chamber through sluices (paddles) until its surface matches the other level, and the boat leaves through the other gate. The older **flash lock** was a single removable weir or gate: opening it let the upper reach rush out, and boats were carried through on the flood (downstream) or hauled up against the current, wasting a great deal of water and sometimes the boat.

The pound lock is credited to Qiao Weiyue, a Song official, in 984 CE: he installed two gates about 250 feet apart, roofed over, on the canal near Huai'an in Jiangsu, to stop barges wrecking on the slipways; Shen Kuo describes such locks in his *Dream Pool Essays* (1088). In Europe, a form of pound lock was built at Vreeswijk in the Netherlands (the sources give 1373 and 1385), the first "true European pound lock" is placed at Damme near Bruges in 1396, and Bertola da Novate built 18 pound locks on the Naviglio di Bereguardo between 1452 and 1458. Mitre gates are attributed to Leonardo da Vinci in the late 15th century. Whether the European lock was invented independently or learnt from China is not established in what I could confirm. The dates come from secondary summaries of Needham, and are flagged unverified.

Scope: the model fills the chamber through paddles that discharge like an orifice; friction in the culverts and leakage are ignored.

refs: Needham, Science and Civilisation in China 4.3 (as cited by Wikipedia “Lock (water navigation)”)

queue.name: The Natural Powers of Water and Wind to Turn Mills

explicitUncertainty.text:
Smeaton's paper, read to the Royal Society in 1759 (he received the Society's Copley Medal for it), reports two series of experiments on working models. In the first he measured water wheels (the results are replayed in 4.5): at the same water and the same fall the overshot wheel does about twice the work of the undershot wheel, and each does best turning slowly. In the second part he tested windmill sails. Because natural wind is too uncertain, he carried the sails round a large circle on an arm, pulling it by hand and regulating the speed with a pendulum, so that the sails met an "artificial wind" of known speed (according to the OCR text, sails of 21 inches radius at a centre speed of 6 ft/s). He measured the load the sails could raise and their turns for different angles of weather (the angle between the sail and the plane of rotation), and concluded that sails set at 55° to the axis were not the best for work and that the angle should vary along the sail, larger near the axis than at the tip. For a sail divided in six parts from the axis outward he gave angles of weather of 18°, 19°, 18°, 16°, 12½° and 7° (the OCR layout of the last two is garbled), and he found that concave sails and a wider leading edge did better still.

He also drew general rules from the windmill tests: the speed of the sails at maximum load is nearly proportional to the wind speed; the load at maximum is nearly, a little less than, proportional to the square of the wind speed; and the work done is nearly, a little less than, proportional to the cube of the wind speed.

What the paper changed: it gave a measured, not argued, answer to a question that engineers had been settling by opinion, and its method (vary one parameter on a model, find the maximum, scale up by stated rules) became a template. I read the paper's text only in an OCR transcription, so every figure quoted here is unverified against the printed page.

queue.name: Smeaton’s water-wheel experiments

explicitUncertainty.text:
In the 1750s the English engineer **John Smeaton** built a working model of a water wheel, with a cistern at a controlled head, a sluice, and a cord that lifted a weight, and measured how much work it did for a given quantity of water. He ran 27 sets of experiments on **undershot** wheels (his Table I) and 16 on **overshot** wheels (Table II), recording for each the power of the water (weight of water used times the height it fell) and the effect (weight raised times the height). He published the results in 1759. The result that mattered: **at the same quantity of water and the same fall, an overshot wheel does about twice the work of an undershot wheel**, and, for each wheel, the maximum effect comes with the wheel turning slowly (for his undershot wheel about two-fifths of the speed of the water). At the time it was widely believed that undershot wheels were the more powerful; Smeaton's measurements are the source of the engineering rule that water's weight, not its impulse, should be used where there is a fall.

How the numbers below were obtained: the two tables were read from an OCR transcription of the 1759 paper (Philosophical Transactions 51, in an online archive), not from page images. The ratio of effect to power was recomputed from the printed Power and Effect columns and agrees with his printed ratios to about 0.05 in 41 of the 43 rows; in rows 10 and 20 of Table I the printed ratio differs by about 0.1, which may be an OCR error or a misprint. The figures called "Smeaton's" are therefore marked unverified against the original pages.

explicitUncertainty.text:
A **marine chronometer** is a clock whose rate is so steady against changes of temperature and ship motion that, once its rate is measured in port, the time it carries can be trusted for weeks. Harrison's H4 (1759) was a large pocket-watch in form with a balance spring (5.8), a bimetallic compensation for temperature, a remontoire to keep the force on the escapement constant, and jewelled pallets. To earn the top prize of the Longitude Act (5.9) it had to be right within about 2 minutes of time at the end of a six-week voyage, i.e. to a few seconds a day.

What the sources support: H4 was carried to Jamaica from November 1761, and sources give a loss of about 5 seconds over 81 days (so, at the time of the landfall, an error of about $1\tfrac14'$ of longitude); this figure is reported but not independently verified, and one skeptical historian doubts it. The 1764 voyage to Barbados gave a second trial. Harrison's later watch designs were copied by Larcum Kendall (K1), and the marine chronometers of Arnold and Earnshaw replaced his design from about 1780.

Scope of the picture: the three clock types have **assumed**, round stabilities (the daily random rate error, the temperature coefficient and the effect of ship motion) chosen to illustrate the argument and are not measurements of any named clock; the tropical warming is a straight ramp.
